This example is different from the previous one. There, a condition beyond the essence and its existence—such as coldness in a paralyzed hand that cannot feel or move—makes something impossible. Here the impossibility comes from the thing’s own level of existence, as with a human form existing in the mind, which cannot be material in that way. In the present case, the requirement of nonexistence may be distinct from the essence, but it is part of its very way of existing. “The nature of reality” means the particular kind of existence that requires matter and time; “the real” is broader. The wording moves from a particular case to the general rule, while the preceding line moved from the general rule to a particular case. — س ره

The author is referring back to the earlier argument, though he will soon discuss further objections to reasoning by contradiction and answer them. The next objection is different: how can an assumption entail what conflicts with it, as when an unlimited distance is said to entail being bounded? — س ره

That is, in those proofs by contradiction. The possibility that may entail an impossibility is possibility in itself. The possibility used in those proofs is possibility in reality: what can occur without contradiction. If something’s being possible in reality entails an impossibility, that proves only that it is not possible in reality. It may still be possible in itself. If it is not possible even in itself, that requires a separate proof. — س ره
This refers to the later necessity, one of the two necessities that surround every possible thing.
This refers to the earlier necessity, expressed by the rule: a thing does not exist until it has become necessary. — س ره

The careful critic takes “inborn preference” in a different sense: just as necessity and impossibility mean that existence or nonexistence must apply to a thing, so the opposing view says that one side is more fitting for a possible thing, without any cause or demand in its essence. Arguments about a thing’s own causal power do not disprove this version. — ه ره

This answers the careful critic’s point. If we say that a possible thing’s own essence causes the preference, then either the possible thing has no reality at all, so it cannot cause anything, or the cause’s effect fails to follow from it. But if we say only that one side fits the thing better, those arguments do not directly apply. Even necessity in itself is not “causation” in the ordinary sense, since the cause and its effect are one. It means that one side fits the thing so fully that it becomes necessary. The claimed preference would be similar, but would stop short of necessity. — س ره

This refers to an inborn preference strong enough to make a thing actual and close off its need for a Creator. Preference may be inborn or come from another, and either kind may or may not be strong enough to make the thing exist. On close examination, all these views fail, though some fail more plainly than others. — س ره

Al-Fārābī’s claim is limited to preference, since that is the topic here. His words “without necessity” cover both a thing coming to exist while existence and nonexistence remain equal, and a thing coming to exist because one side is preferred but not necessary. He does not mention that existence might come about with no preference at all, as that is already included in the first case. — س ره

The first case concerns preference strong enough to make the thing actual. This case concerns a preference too weak to do that. The thing would then occur without being brought about by its essence or by anything separate, since the argument assumes an existence sequence without necessity. — س ره

This is another reason the second case is worse. The existence of a possible thing is not its essence and therefore needs a cause. If the essence makes existence preferred, it is the cause of the thing’s being described as existent. The thing could still fail to exist, however, because the preference does not make existence necessary. Its nonexistence would then be possible even while its essence—the alleged cause of existence—remained. The argument is a proof, not a debate that depends on the opponent accepting the author’s premise: the opponent has already assumed that the thing exists without any cause. — س ره

There are three possible states. In the view defended here, the less-favored side is always impossible and the favored side necessary in itself. In the opposing view, the less-favored side has only a non-necessary disadvantage and can still occur; the favored side has only a non-necessary advantage. The third state is that the favored side has a non-necessary advantage while the less-favored side is impossible. The author argues that only a necessary disadvantage could make the less-favored side impossible, but the opponent has assumed a mere preference. — س ره

Someone may say that this changes the assumption, since a preference short of necessity has become an impossibility, even if not an impossibility in itself. The reply is that the impossibility applies to nonexistence only when it is qualified by being less favored. It does not apply to the essence by itself. The essence remains possible, and the impossibility that belongs to the added description comes through something else. — س ره

Someone may object that the less-favored feature depends on the essence, and what depends on something also depends on the thing it depends on. The answer is that the preference does depend on the essence, as does the preference for existence. But neither preference is necessary in itself; each can be absent. So the impossibility and necessity that arise from them can also be absent. There is no contradiction. — س ره
“Some possible things” means certain possible essences. The phrase continues the opening of the next argument. — س ره
Copies differ here: some say “before the commentary on philosophy,” while others say “before philosophy matured.”
This example differs in no important way from the one just given. That is why the author answers it, and the next claim, together by saying that both are false. — س ره
This means stable things, such as substances. — ه ره
In other words: if you accept this for cause and effect, accept it also for an essence’s supposed preference for existence. — س ره
These are the two mistaken claims: the one about things that pass away, and the one about a cause that waits for conditions before bringing about its effect. — ه ره

A clearer way to put the point is: necessity gives a thing independence, and impossibility does the same in its own way. A thing needs something else because neither existence nor nonexistence is necessary for it. If origination—either as a condition or as part of the reason for need—were added to that reason, it would still be considered only for something possible in itself. A necessary or impossible thing would already be independent. So the argument finally returns to possibility. This proof also shows that origination alone cannot even be part of the reason for needing a cause. The next proof applies to all the views. — س ره
The word means “of the relation.” — س ره
If origination is a condition, it comes one step later still, because a condition must itself be in place before what depends on it. — س ره

Possibility is the way the imagined idea of existence relates to an essence in the mind. This is why we can call an essence possible before it exists. Origination, by contrast, means that the existence given to an essence was preceded by nonexistence. It therefore comes after the act that gives the essence existence.
Many copies read “preference,” but “being preferred” is the correct reading. The word “preference” is used only to echo the earlier wording. — س ره
Some copies omit the phrase “in relation to.”

The examples of the two cups, two loaves, and two roads were used by al-Ashʿarī to argue that one equal option may be chosen without a reason. But a few examples cannot prove a general rule. Perhaps the point was only to argue against an opponent, not to establish the general claim. Also, for al-Ashʿarī, God acts and people are compelled; so any reason for the choice must lie with God, not with the person choosing. The same is true for those who hold that God creates the act while people still have some role in it. Demanding a reason only from the person’s point of view fits the view that people act independently. The author’s reply is that God may have hidden causes in creation: He may know, for instance, that the second road leads to a pit or a wild animal, and direct the person toward the first to protect them. Even when people act, they may in some nearby actions be instruments through which God or an angel acts. — س ره

Their argument is that the same cause would apply equally to both matching things, as would their essence and anything that follows from it. Any separate factor would also seem to apply to both. If the differing factor were itself separate, the same question would arise again, leading to an endless chain. The reply is that an endless chain of changing conditions does not imply that the chain has always existed. One thing may be prepared by earlier conditions in its own matter, while the other is prepared by different conditions. If we ask what explains the difference between those conditions, the answer points to still earlier conditions in their respective materials, and so on. There is no endless chain of things existing all at once, because material conditions change. Or the material itself may be the factor that makes the two outcomes differ. If someone asks why one material is prepared one way and another differently, the answer is that each material is part of what makes the thing that particular thing. Without those differences, the two would not be two separate things. The commentator notes that the argument’s use of “matching things” is itself questionable if there is truly no difference between them. — س ره
This is mistaken: “being essential” is not the whole essence. It is a general, incidental idea in the mind. — س ره

The point is that what is known depends, in one way, on God’s knowledge: the fixed forms of things are known by Him. God’s knowledge, which is one with His single essence, follows those forms in what they require of themselves; in that sense, the forms are truly described by their own essential features. His knowledge, however, is too exalted to be described by them except in a dependent way. The forms and realities are likewise described by existence, knowledge, and other perfections only in a dependent way. So divine knowledge is, in one respect, dependent on what it knows and, in another, the source on which those realities depend. — ن ره

One could explain it this way: the world’s existence is “by chance” in the sense that it exists through another, not through itself. Everything returns to God; “everything perishes except His face.” “O You who are, You who are nothing but You: everything apart from God is false.” — ن ره

This is the existence itself. How, then, could existence be what comes about only incidentally, rather than directly? Earlier the author reported Suhrawardī’s view that existence is only an idea, as are necessity through another and similar concepts. He did not accept this for existence or for necessity through another. Perhaps here “necessity through another” means the way a relation is qualified, not necessity itself. — س ره

The author will later explain that saying things happen by chance conflicts with necessary links in existence. It works only if one denies necessity and impossibility altogether: if a necessary link existed, one thing would depend on another through that link, and chance would disappear. The debaters’ appeals to “producing what already exists” and “joining opposites” overlook this point. — ط

The author does not answer the supposed problem here because “while” is taken to mean that cause and effect exist at the same time. There is no problem with the cause and its effect existing together. — س ره

This would put the cause’s action and its effect at the same level in the order of what things are. But that cannot be right. The cause acts on what the thing is, considered in itself; at that level the thing has no separate identity that could stand beside the cause as an equal. Considered as existing or nonexistent, it comes after the cause’s existence or nonexistence. — س ره

The point is that saying “the cause acts on the essence as it is in itself” does not mean that the essence itself is directly made. It is the place where the effect appears, or is called the effect in another sense. The author explains this in The Divine Witnesses, when he divides existence into the real, the general, and the limited. The essence is like a footstool or an image of existence. — س ره

Origination means that existence is preceded by nonexistence. So this view places the cause’s action in the interval between the time of nonexistence and the time of existence, not in either state. It is a difficult view because it does not apply to things created directly, on their account, but only to the natural world as a whole. — س ره

They choose the view that the cause acts while the effect does not exist, then say that no opposites are joined because the cause acts in the first moment and the effect exists in the second. This is simply mistaken: it makes the time before the effect exists the cause’s time of action. — س ره
Yes, but this is a simple negative statement; or we can say, “The human being no longer remains.” — س ره
The correct wording is “or the relation being described as existent.” — س ره
That is, through the cause. — س ره
That is, a simple, undivided thing, like the undivided knowledge of God. They mean the simple reality named by “being described as existent,” which the mind analyzes into parts. — س ره

They missed the case where being described as something is not an independent thing, but is not itself noticed as an object. This is suggested by their claim that being described as something is itself an essence, though it is not really an essence. It is simply an essence being described as existent. It is like saying that a thing’s coming to be is itself a thing that has come to be. — س ره

The difficulty is this: if existence alone is real in its own right, then every true statement that matches neither the outside world nor our minds considered as mental states would be impossible. One example is “the effect’s absence is caused by the cause’s absence.” This statement is true, even if nobody happens to think it. But it does not match anything in the outside world, since absence is nothing and has no external reality.

The usual answer is that such truths correspond to “reality as such” (nafs al-amr), rather than to the outside world or the mind. Philosophers say that “reality as such” includes everything in the outside world, and overlaps with what is in the mind while also reaching beyond it. Some explain it to mean the thing itself: saying that a thing is such-and-such “in itself” means that the thing itself is such-and-such; the wording puts “the thing” in place of “it.”

But this explanation does not solve the problem. If “the thing itself” means its real existence, the original difficulty returns. If it means the thing’s essence, distinct from its existence, that cannot be right either, because nothing besides existence is real. Others explain “reality as such” as the World of Command: a universal, immaterial intellect containing the forms of all true statements. But if those forms are direct knowledge—things present to that intellect—then they are just the external realities themselves, and would not match a statement such as “the effect’s absence is caused by the cause’s absence.” The problem remains. If they are ideas in that intellect, there is no reason to posit them, since similar ideas already exist in our minds; and again the problem remains.

The better answer is this: what is real in its own right is actual existence, and it is what truly exists. Every true fact belongs to it. Essences are ways existence appears to our rational minds. So the mind is forced to extend the idea of “existence” to essences as well, then make whatever true judgments it must about them. In this way, the concept of “existence” or “being” comes to apply more broadly, both to real existence and to essences.

Then the mind is forced to take a further step: it applies the bare idea of being real to every abstract concept it has had to form, such as nonexistence, unity, action, and potentiality. It also accepts the judgments about these concepts that reason requires. The place the mind imagines for reality in this broadest sense is what we call “reality as such.” The author will return to this later, God willing, in the discussions of mental existence and other topics. — ط
Rather, the essence is established as an object of the mind’s consideration, and so becomes possible. — س ره
That is, the “natural universal,” another name for an essence. — س ره

Existence’s need for a cause is essential to it, as the author says. What is essential in this way is not itself explained by a cause. The claim that possibility is the cause of need applies to essences. Here, “cause” means a step in the explanation, and the need belongs to the essence indirectly. If we mean the need that exists in dependent beings, then “possibility” means dependence or poverty, and the point returns to what we have said: this need is essential and has no further cause. — س ره
That is, a body is finite in general, and each of its particular forms of existence is limited in its own way. — ن ره

Here, “eternity” means only a dependent, derivative kind of permanence, not existence that is eternal in itself or independently. God is far above having a partner. The reality described as eternal in this way belongs to the World of Command, not to the created world. God has real attributes of perfection that are identical with the depth of His essence, and relational attributes that lie beyond that depth. Their being “additional” in this relational sense does not conflict with saying that His attributes are identical with Him in every respect. Complete devotion to God’s oneness denies any attribute added to Him, whether relational or real. Consider this carefully: the point is subtle, and few grasp it fully. — ن ره
Existence is the relation itself, not a thing that has a relation. It cannot be separated from this relation, just as a thing cannot be separated from itself. — ن ره
This refers to the earlier discussion, where the author first established an aspect of permanence for some possible existences—those belonging to the World of Command—then denied it. — ن ره

The example is imperfect because, in the case under discussion, there is no fixed thing like a body that receives a manifestation of God as a body receives the sun. Things are manifestations of His light and displays of His beauty and majesty. Nothing is already established before this manifestation; there are only its levels and forms. — ن ره

Some effects have one cause for coming into being and another for continuing to exist. A building, for example, comes into being through construction, but lasts because its material is dry and firm. Other effects have the same cause for both, as when a mold gives water its shape. The world, in relation to God, belongs to this second kind: God is necessary in Himself and necessary in every respect. The world does not belong to the first kind. So anyone who says that, if God could cease to exist, the world would still continue without Him should be silenced outright. — س ره
This excludes mere preparatory causes. Their role is called causation only in a loose sense; it is accidental, not genuine causation. — ن ره

This can mean one of two things. First, the soul may become able to do without the body and its use once it has reached full development. This is the natural end of life. Or the body may lose its ability to receive the soul before the soul has reached full development, because of some outside accident. That is a violent or untimely death. — ن ره

What the builder directly causes is the movement of his own body: his soul moves and sets his limbs in motion. The exact joining of parts, such as bricks and stones, into a particular form happens only as an indirect result of his powers. This kind of indirect influence is called chance or coincidence. — ن ره
That is, in terms of kind or type. — ن ره

As you can see, the sea of matter runs out because there is no matter that exists separately on its own. God’s words of existence do not run out, because His giving of existence never stops, He never withholds His mercy, and He cannot be silent. The same applies to the seven seas. — س ره
At that point, the supposed deciding factor is still equally related to both sides. So what seemed to be a preference is, in truth, an equal relation. Think carefully. — ن ره

You may ask: if existence already has the advantage, how can the two outcomes still be equally open? I answer: even a cause that will eventually make one outcome necessary leaves both outcomes open until it has done all that is needed. A cause that merely favors existence has not ruled out every way the effect could fail to exist. The preference, considered without the final purpose or condition that settles the outcome, has left both possibilities open. To claim that the preference already belongs to existence is to confuse what the mind considers with what has actually happened. The thing does not yet exist. As we have seen, possibility is not a separate state alongside the thing's existence or nonexistence; nor is a mere preference.

Consider the argument another way. If a preference truly fixed one outcome, that outcome would be necessary—contrary to the assumption. The preference is itself something that may occur or not occur and therefore also needs an explanation. Al-Sayyid al-Sharif objects: why should the greater weight supplied by an outside cause not suffice for the favored outcome? What is obviously impossible, he says, is for two equally balanced outcomes to occur without a reason, or for the less favored one to occur. I reply that if the favored outcome actually happens, the supposed mere preference has given way to what makes its occurrence necessary. Beforehand, necessity is something we understand; when the possible thing exists, it exists through the necessity supplied by its cause. Its actual existence reveals that the cause made it necessary.

You may reply that, for us, existence reveals necessity, but for those who accept mere preference it reveals only preference. We mean by necessity nothing more than what makes the thing truly exist. If you choose to call that 'preference,' our disagreement is only about a name; you might as well call it 'possibility.' But how could actual existence, which excludes nonexistence, show only a preference that still allows nonexistence?

To say that a possible thing comes into existence through a preference that has not reached necessity is like saying that a person reaches a rooftop merely by thinking about it, deciding to climb, setting up a ladder, and stepping on every rung except the last one. The final part of the complete cause is still missing. However many incomplete conditions have been met, they do not settle whether the person reaches the roof. Even endlessly many such preferences would not explain why the cause brings about existence rather than leaving the thing nonexistent. That would still be choosing one outcome without what decides it. I have explained this at length because the distinction is easy to miss. Do not let it escape you. — س ره

Saying that the sides cannot be equal because the preference points towards existence confuses what the mind considers with what exists outside the mind. Existence has not yet occurred in the outside world, so the possible thing’s existence is no more actual than its nonexistence. As explained earlier, possibility applies only when we consider the thing in itself, not to its actual absence or to its actual existence—whether outside the mind, in the mind, now, or in the future. Preference, too, has meaning only at that level. It is not yet an actual state.

Another way to put the argument is this: if the preference is not equal and truly belongs to one side, then that side has become necessary through its cause. But the claim under discussion assumes that no necessity has been reached. Also, preference itself is one of the things the mind can consider; it too may occur or fail to occur. Its own occurrence would therefore need a preference.

A later commentator raises this objection: Why can’t the favored side occur simply because an outside cause has made it more likely? This does not seem obviously impossible; what is obviously impossible is that one of two equally likely sides, or the less likely side, should occur. The answer is that when the favored side actually occurs, this goes beyond mere preference. How is it different from saying that the cause made it necessary? In the mind, necessity is distinct from existence and is considered before it. Outside the mind, necessity is the existence itself. So when we know that a possible thing exists, we know that its cause made it necessary.

Someone might reply: “That is your view. Those who accept mere preference without necessity say that existence shows only that the cause favored it.” We answer that by “necessity” we mean whatever grounds the judgment that the thing exists. If you call this “preference,” then we disagree only about the name. Call it “possibility” if you wish. But how could actual existence, which cannot be absent, show a preference that can fail to occur, even if its absence is less likely? Existence and necessity cannot fail to be; mere preference can.

To say that a possible thing can exist through a preference that falls short of necessity is like saying that someone can reach a roof by imagining the result, deciding to do it, wanting it, setting up a ladder, and climbing every rung except the last. The result would occur even though the final part of the complete cause was missing. Having many conditions and incomplete causes in place does not remove the equal chance of reaching the roof or not reaching it, when the outcome is considered in relation to the person who acts. Those conditions are only being considered in the mind. Even infinitely many weak preferences would not settle what the person brings about. For the person to produce existence rather than nonexistence would still be a choice without a reason. The author expands the discussion because it is easy to misunderstand. — س ره

Calling the concept “existent” an essential feature of a real instance of existence is slightly imprecise. That is why the author adds that it must be true as long as the reality exists. As explained earlier, existence is not a species, a general kind, a dividing feature, a universal, or a particular. The real point is that the concept of existence is an abstract idea the mind draws from descriptions; as a concept, it has no reality outside the mind. If it did, existence, whose very nature is to be outside the mind, would itself exist in the mind in the same way it exists outside. It would then have one nature in the mind and another outside it, and would become an essence equally open to being and not being. That is impossible. — ط

The argument is that if nonexistence were possible while the thing exists, opposite claims would be true at once. That is impossible in itself. Whatever entails something impossible in itself is also impossible in itself. So existence would be necessary in itself. — س ره
For this speaker, the condition is the essence’s relation to its maker. — س ره

This answer works if the condition is part of what we call the subject. The claim that a cause must exist for its effect works differently: there the cause explains why the effect exists. The reply to the earlier scholar changes the objection rather than answering it directly. The author says 'even if the argument were complete' because it is not. Possibility and impossibility concern existence and nonexistence in general, not some special kind of either. Motion, for example, can exist, but not as something fixed and unchanging. A thing impossible in itself must be nonexistent, not merely absent in one particular way. Yet the other scholar speaks of 'nonexistence while the thing exists,' which is a special case. Moreover, he treats 'while it exists' as a condition on the denial of existence. It really qualifies the subject, for the subject is already 'the existing essence.' Adding the condition to the denial repeats what the subject already says. An essence considered as existing cannot, while it exists, be nonexistent. Its opposite—existence—is therefore necessary. — س ره

There is another problem. The phrase “nonexistent while it exists” makes “while it exists” sound like a condition on the claim that the thing is absent. But it is really a condition on the subject: it means the essence is being considered as existing at that time. So adding the condition to nonexistence repeats the same idea. An essence that exists at a given time cannot be absent at that time; its opposite, existence, must hold. — س ره
This can be so when the opposite side is nonexistence; when the opposite side is existence, it may be impossible. — س ره

The essence considered by itself can receive existence, and existence belongs to it in that respect. The opposite claim, nonexistence, concerns the essence under the condition that it exists. This reading fits the view of the Imam and is also suggested by the author’s later words. — س ره

In the second way, the difference comes from applying a condition. Here, the difference comes from the condition itself. A difference made by adding a condition is weaker than one made by the condition itself, though both involve a condition. — ن ره
This is a proof, not just an argument meant to trap the other side. So it does not show that the author rejects the view that existence is real in itself. — س ره

This rule is very useful. If a possible thing exists at one time, it cannot be absent at that time, since it must exist while it exists. It cannot be removed from another time when it was never there. Nor can it be absent from reality altogether: for reality as a whole to lack it, it would have to be absent at every level, which is not the case. This is why things are said to remain fixed in relation to the higher sources, and even more so in relation to the First Source. Each thing is present to Him at its own level, with no fading or loss. One of God's beautiful names addresses Him as 'You from whose treasures nothing is diminished.' God's knowledge does not change. This concerns an essence insofar as it has become real. As for a particular real existence, nonexistence cannot belong to it: a thing cannot receive its own opposite, and existence has no separate underlying subject on which its contrary could arrive and replace it. Understand this. — س ره

This is an important principle with further consequences. For example, every material being implies the existence of a corresponding being that does not depend on matter, is of the same order, and oversees it. Why? If the material being has a place in reality as a whole, it cannot be lost from that whole; and in that respect it cannot undergo any change. Every change involves some loss of what was there. Yet every material thing, precisely because it is material, can change in some way. So at every level of material beings there must be a corresponding being free from matter, loss, and change.

Some Western students of nature, noticing something of this principle, supposed that a thing might eventually cease to need a cause. They reached that conclusion because they considered only causes made of matter. They overlooked two points. First, a material being's relation to reality as a whole does not do away with the relations among material beings themselves. Second, not every cause is a material cause. There is also the cause that acts and produces an effect, which anything that depends on another for its existence still needs. We shall establish this later. — ط

This idea led some Western scientists to wonder whether the need for a cause might end if “cause” meant only a material cause. But they missed two points. First, the relation between a material thing and reality as a whole does not cancel the relations between material things themselves. Second, causes are not only material; there is also the cause that brings a possible thing into being, and no possible thing can do without it. This will be proved later. — ط
Here, “reality altogether” means reality in general, without limiting it to one level or a particular set of levels. — ن ره

On the view that each kind has a higher, guiding reality, every essence has one kind of possibility in the realm of intellect, but may have two in the material world. According to this view, the higher realities of kinds are each represented by a single individual, while in the material world a kind may have many members. The difference comes from matter and the further conditions it needs. — س ره

This is a hidden point that few understand. The movement at issue is a thing’s passage from potential to actual. This passage must ultimately rest on a simple reality that changes from within itself, not because another thing changes it. Otherwise, the chain of changing things would go on without end. This simple, ever-flowing present is the timeless order that connects what changes with what does not. Time measures ordinary motion: the gradual change of something that receives new actuality from an active source. Time is the very reality of this changing thing as it passes step by step from potential to actual. A sequence of events in time leads, in one direction, to the timeless order, which joins the eternity beyond time. The active source remains; what receives its action begins and ends. So we speak of the source’s continuous giving, not of the world as a product that has continued forever. — ن ره

Some things brought into being through direct creation are joined to time and place without themselves changing gradually. The heavenly spheres, for example, are living beings whose matter is formed by souls that have no parts of measurable size. A sphere's nature and its soul are one in existence, though we can consider them separately. Its measurable parts belong to its body insofar as its body is matter, not insofar as it belongs to a general kind. Such a being is alive by its nature and does not die through the usual process in which one bodily form replaces another. It may cease to appear, but that is not the same as dying. Disappearance is broader than decay, just as existence is broader than coming into being. A link with time and place that does not involve gradual change can end without one thing being destroyed by another. Existence itself cannot be destroyed, for that would require a change in God's knowledge—far be it from Him. On the day when the heavens are rolled up like a scroll, their disappearance is the drawing back of what was spread out; what seemed mixed is no longer mixed, and what comes into view does so in a new form. Consider this carefully. — ن ره
Some copies read “or things that are desired.”
All this follows from the view that existence is a real, graded reality, with levels ordered by completeness and lack. The highest level is God. — ط

If 'possibility' here means being dependent on another, the comparison is clear: dependence stands to necessity as lack stands to completeness. Dependent existences are described as luminous because their very reality consists in being connected to and supported by another; that connection is not something added to them. But if 'possibility' means neither existence nor nonexistence being necessary, or means that both remain equally open, then we are speaking of a feature of an essence, not of an existence. Since it is not the same kind of thing as necessary existence, we can call it a lack only in comparison with sheer nonexistence and nothingness. — س ره

The discussion is about readiness, not about the sperm as the thing that has readiness. The sperm is only an example. A readiness-quality depends on its subject. So it is actual in one respect and potential in another. Basic possibility, by contrast, is pure potential: its subject is not actual, whether in existence or nonexistence. — س ره
This is not the same as saying that something is possible because its occurrence would involve no contradiction. — ه ره

On this view, readiness is only a relation. The mixture in a sperm is a bodily quality, and a courtyard is a space. Here, “coexist by chance” means that they happen to accompany one another, without any necessary connection. — س ره

The difficulty is that comparing something with another thing requires the first thing to be visible and distinct to the person making the comparison. That cannot happen in the situation being described. — ن ره

If the explanation were as stated, then all impossible things and all complex forms of absolute nonexistence would be known and could be discussed. What, then, would remain of the claim that absolute nonexistence and what is impossible in itself cannot be known or discussed? The real question is how we can form a concept of something that has no distinction, knowledge, or report about it at all, and then make claims about it. — ن ره
